title: Photos and voice notes from the field
scenario:
You run operations for a company that services heating systems. Every day, 40 technicians send photos and voice notes from customer sites. Office staff then type everything into the job system by hand. Your director asks you to plan how AI can help, using a model that can read images and transcribe audio.

The exhibit lists the ideas the team collected.
exhibit:
Ideas from the team

1. Read the pressure value from photos of boiler gauges.
2. Count spare parts on van-shelf photos, so we can stop the monthly stock count.
3. Transcribe technicians' voice notes into job reports.
4. A new phone line where an AI voice reads out appointment times to customers.

questions.prompt: Which idea should you push back on, based on the vendors' documented limits?

options.text: Idea 1, because models can't read any numbers in photos of physical gauges at all.
options.explanation: Vision models can read visible text and numbers. Gauge photos need clear images and a check, but the idea itself is workable.

options.text: Idea 3, because models can't handle audio, so voice notes always need typing by hand.
options.explanation: OpenAI and Gemini both document transcription of recorded audio. This idea is a good fit.

options.text: Idea 2, because counts from images can be approximate and can't replace a stock count.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's and OpenAI's guides both say object counts can be approximate. AI counts may help spot gaps, but not replace the real count.

options.text: Idea 4, because AI voices are banned from talking to customers by every vendor's policy.
options.explanation: OpenAI's policies allow it, with a clear disclosure that the voice is AI-generated. It is not banned.

questions.prompt: In a trial of idea 1, the model misreads about one gauge in ten. Most errors come from dark, tilted or far-away photos. What is the best next step?

options.text: Give technicians a photo rule (close, upright, lit) and tell the model to write "unclear" if unsure.
options.explanation: Right. The vendors' tips ask for clear, upright images. Letting the model say "unclear" turns a hidden error into a visible gap that a person can fix.

options.text: Ask the model to give its best guess for every gauge, so the job system never has an empty field.
options.explanation: A forced guess hides the bad photos. A wrong pressure value in a report is worse than a blank that someone fills in.

options.text: Send each photo at the highest possible size, since a bigger file always gives a correct reading.
options.explanation: Size can't fix a dark, tilted photo, and larger images cost more tokens. Anthropic's guide shows token cost growing with image size.

options.text: Drop the idea, because one error in ten shows that image reading is not ready for any work use.
options.explanation: The errors have a clear cause you can fix. Fix the input first, then measure again.

questions.prompt: In idea 3, part codes like "HX-40" and the brand name "Thermaline" are often written wrong in the transcripts. What should you change?

options.text: Ask technicians to spell out every part code letter by letter in their notes.
options.explanation: That slows down every technician, every day. Give the transcription the context instead.

options.text: Give the transcription a short prompt with the brand and part codes, then check new errors.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's guide says a prompt can improve product names, technical terms and acronyms. It also says to check that hints don't add words nobody said.

options.text: Have office staff retype the full transcript, since automatic transcripts are always unreliable.
options.explanation: The errors are in a known, small set of words. A targeted fix keeps most of the time savings.

options.text: Run every voice note through the transcription twice, then keep whichever version is longer.
options.explanation: The longer transcript is not the more correct one. Without the right terms, both runs can get the codes wrong.

questions.prompt: For idea 4, what must the phone line do if it uses OpenAI's text-to-speech?

options.text: Use a voice that sounds exactly like one of the human office staff, so customers feel at home.
options.explanation: That hides the fact that the voice is AI. OpenAI's policies require the opposite: a clear disclosure.

options.text: Only run outside office hours, since AI voices may not be used during the normal workday.
options.explanation: No such rule exists in the docs. The requirement is about telling listeners the voice is AI.

options.text: Get written consent from each customer before the first call, by letter or by email.
options.explanation: The requirement in OpenAI's guide is a clear disclosure to the people listening. A letter before the first call is not what it asks for.

options.text: Clearly tell callers that the voice they hear is AI-generated, not a human voice.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's text-to-speech guide says its usage policies require this disclosure to end users.
